_comment: Guided tour for the RICS precision planner. Declarative AutoForm view (precision.view.json); steps target bound attributes and the result plot/table titles. This tool takes no data at all — it is used *before* the measurement — so the awaited step is an edit rather than a Run. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: The one tool here you use before the measurement
steps.text:
Everything else in ChiSurf analyses data you already have. This predicts what precision a raster-scan correlation measurement would reach — from the settings you intend to use and the diffusion coefficient you expect.

It takes no data at all. The point is to find out, before you book the microscope, whether your intended scan can resolve the difference you care about.

Five steps.

steps.title: Start from the D you expect
steps.text:
This is the awkward part of the question, and there is no way around it: where the optimum lies depends on the D you are trying to measure — the number you do not have yet.

So put in what you expect, and treat the answer as conditional on it. If you are unsure within a factor of three, run it at both ends: that is far more informative than one confident number.

await.hint: Enter the diffusion coefficient you expect.

steps.title: Why there is a minimum in the middle
steps.text:
The dwell time trades two failures against each other:

Too fast — the molecule has barely moved between neighbouring pixels, so the correlation carries almost no information about D, and few photons land in each pixel anyway.
Too slow — it has already decorrelated by the time the next pixel is read, so the correlation has decayed before you sample it.

Neither end is a small penalty. The curve is plotted on log axes precisely because a badly matched dwell is wrong by orders of magnitude, and on a linear axis the whole usable 2–10 % range flattens into a line.

steps.title: The optics set the length scale the scan is compared against
steps.text:
The beam waist and the pixel size are what turn a dwell time into a distance the molecule may have travelled — so they decide where the trough sits just as much as D does.

Getting the pixel size wrong here does not make the curve look wrong; it moves the optimum without any indication that it has.

steps.title: Read the trough as an order of magnitude, not a setting
steps.text:
Your own dwell is marked on the curve, and the status line turns it into a sentence — how good it is, and how much better the best dwell would be.

Rough guide: below 5 % means differences between conditions will be measurable; 5–20 % is usable for a large effect; above that the experiment is unlikely to answer the question.

Two honest limits. Each point is itself a Monte-Carlo estimate — about 10 % at the default repeat count — so the position of the minimum is an order of magnitude and not a value to dial in. And precision is quoted per frame count, not per unit time: a slower scan in this comparison is also a longer acquisition, so read the table's implied line and frame times before choosing.

The ? button has the rest.
